title: Live streaming
brief: Streamers broadcast live and thousands watch together, with a chat on the side. Everyone wants the same piece of video at the same second, so nothing can be saved for later. When a big streamer goes live, the whole audience arrives at once.

clarify.q: How far behind real time may the video be?
clarify.a: About 3 to 5 seconds. Viewers tolerate that, but not freezes.

clarify.q: Is chat as important as the video?
clarify.a: Almost. Chat messages must arrive in a second or two, and a huge chat is mostly many people reading the same few messages.

clarify.q: What if a streamer is raided by another channel?
clarify.a: The audience can grow ten times in minutes. It will happen on the busiest night.

clarify.q: Do viewers need to sign in?
clarify.a: To chat, yes. To watch, no.

requirements.users: 1 million viewers a month, thousands live at once
notes: Each live piece is 1 MB and covers 2 seconds.
One live request stands for a 2-second piece of the broadcast, about 1 MB (approx.).

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Live pieces per second at peak
Chat messages per second at peak

hints: Everyone wants the same piece of video at the same second. What does that mean for caching?
A CDN with miss collapsing turns thousands of identical requests into one trip to the origin. Chat needs open connections, not normal web requests: use a websocket gateway.
Chat can degrade without consuming the resources needed for live playback. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Live video is cacheable for a few seconds and cacheable by everybody at once, which makes a CDN with collapsed misses the whole story for the picture. Chat is a different problem: many open connections and every message copied to every viewer. Run them as two separate systems so a chat flood never freezes the video.

designs.name: Two paths: picture on the CDN, chat on sockets
designs.why: The CDN and shield merge all viewers into a single stream of requests to the ingest storage. Chat flows over a websocket gateway to a chat service, with pub/sub copying each message to the gateways that need it. The two paths share nothing.

tradeoffs: A 5-second cache is long enough to merge thousands of identical requests and short enough to keep the stream live. A longer cache would make the video lag.
Collapsing misses protects the origin but makes everyone wait if the origin is slow. That is the right trade for live video, because they all wait together.
Splitting chat from video costs more machines but means a spam attack on chat cannot freeze the picture.
Chat history can lose a few messages without anyone noticing. Account data cannot. Treat them differently.
When a region fails, viewers in other regions keep watching only if the CDN and ingest are already spread across regions.
editorial.realWorld: Live platforms commonly run 3 to 10 seconds behind real time (approx.). One top streamer can hold well over 100,000 viewers at once, while the chat for that stream carries hundreds of messages per second.

correctness.prompt: Live streaming: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Distribute live segments within a bounded delay and isolate chat pressure. Network arrival order is not media order; buffering consumes the live-delay budget. Late live media may be useless; recovery must preserve decoder state and bounded lag. Chat can degrade without consuming the resources needed for live playback.

fields.label: Step 1. Segment 42 reaches an edge after segment 43. What does playback use?
options: Sequence numbers and a bounded reorder buffer
fields.explanation: Network arrival order is not media order; buffering consumes the live-delay budget.

fields.label: Step 2. A segment misses its playback deadline. What should retries do?
options: Stop retrying stale media and recover at a decodable boundary
Retry until every old segment arrives
fields.explanation: Late live media may be useless; recovery must preserve decoder state and bounded lag.

fields.label: Step 3. A chat flood fills shared workers. What protects the stream?
options: Put both into one unbounded queue
Separate budgets and backpressure for chat and video
fields.explanation: Chat can degrade without consuming the resources needed for live playback.

correctness.responsibility: Distribute live segments within a bounded delay and isolate chat pressure.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 800 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $76234. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
